title: Lights off. What did the robot see?
lead: A researcher dimmed the room where a robot moved a ball into a basket. One recorded view barely became darker, probably because of the cameras’ automatic settings.

news.title: Check whether the stack will fall first
news.summary: Japan's NTT made software compare what could happen after different robot movements. In a small experiment, the check helped a robot place objects on a shelf more successfully.
news.details: NTT researchers built a world model: software that predicts changes around a robot. It estimates object properties from images and uses the laws of motion to help generate video predictions of a load falling or staying in place.
news.technical_novelty: Japan's NTT made software compare what could happen after different robot movements. In a small experiment, the check helped a robot place objects on a shelf more successfully.
news.engineering_impact: NTT wants to apply this approach to airport baggage. It has not yet shown that result on an operating baggage line. Real bags vary in shape and weight, while the reported experiment used a small test setup.
news.limitations: The company wants to apply this approach to airport baggage. It has not yet shown that result on an operating baggage line. Real bags vary in shape and weight, while the reported experiment used a small test setup.
news.evidence_status: The company itself reports the tests, specifications or plans. The announcement supplies no independent verification.
news.body:
Putting something on a shelf can go wrong even when the arm reaches the right place. A neighboring object might fall. Researchers at Japan's NTT tried calculating the consequences of several movements before choosing which one to use.

They built a world model: software that predicts changes around a robot. It estimates object position, speed and other properties from images. Calculations using the laws of motion then help produce a video of a possible outcome, such as a load staying in place or falling.

A small robot tested the idea by stacking objects on a shelf. Reported success rose from 73.1% to 92.3%. Those shares are roughly 73 and 92 successes out of a hundred; the announcement does not say that exactly a hundred attempts were made.

The company wants to apply this approach to airport baggage. It has not yet shown that result on an operating baggage line. Real bags vary in shape and weight, while the reported experiment used a small test setup.

news.title: Wheels help engineers test a robot's motors
news.summary: Boston Dynamics engineers replaced a humanoid robot's feet with wheels. They used it to check how real motors carry out movements learned on a computer.
news.details: In the Boston Dynamics experiment, robot movements are first tried in simulation, a computer experiment. Software learns using scores for its results, while measurements of real motors help keep the computer model from granting them unrealistic strength.
news.technical_novelty: Boston Dynamics engineers replaced a humanoid robot's feet with wheels. They used it to check how real motors carry out movements learned on a computer.
news.engineering_impact: Some movements followed recordings of a person. During a quick sideways movement, the robot rolled where the person slid their feet. The experiment does not tell us motor lifetime: the company gives no number of hours under these loads. For reference, the robot is called Atlas.
news.limitations: Some movements followed recordings of a person. During a quick sideways movement, the robot rolled where the person slid their feet. The experiment does not tell us motor lifetime: the company gives no number of hours under these loads. For reference, the robot is called Atlas.
news.evidence_status: The company itself reports the tests, specifications or plans. The announcement supplies no independent verification.
news.body:
The robot rolls, turns and stops sharply. Its wheels are not the launch of a new machine for sale. Boston Dynamics engineers wanted to test motors while they worked quickly and pushed hard for sustained periods.

The movements are first tried in a simulation, a computer experiment with a virtual robot. Software receives scores for the results and gradually finds useful movements. This is called reinforcement learning. If a virtual motor is stronger than the real one, the learned movement might fail on the laboratory floor.

The team therefore measured the real actuators, the devices that move robot parts. They adjusted the computer model to match those measurements. A special adapter attached each wheel to a drive that had previously moved a foot.

Some movements followed recordings of a person. During a quick sideways movement, the robot rolled where the person slid their feet. The experiment does not tell us motor lifetime: the company gives no number of hours under these loads. For reference, the robot is called Atlas.

news.title: Why a dark room did not make a dark picture
news.summary: A researcher in Denmark tested a robot in normal and low light. One recorded view barely became darker, probably because of the cameras’ automatic settings.
news.details: Simon Cowling tested four robot-arm controllers. Success was 20 out of 40 attempts in normal light and 19 out of 40 in low light, but the camera pictures did not dim nearly as much as the room.
news.technical_novelty: A researcher in Denmark tested a robot in normal and low light. One recorded view barely became darker, probably because of the cameras’ automatic settings.
news.engineering_impact: That setting probably helped, but no separate comparison switched the automatic control off. The test therefore did not show how the programs handle genuinely dark pictures. Camera settings matter here because the program receives its pictures through the camera, rather than seeing the room directly.
news.limitations: That setting probably helped, but no separate comparison switched the automatic control off. The test therefore did not show how the programs handle genuinely dark pictures. Camera settings matter here because the program receives its pictures through the camera, rather than seeing the room directly.
news.evidence_status: The researchers describe their own tests. Repetition by another team has not been confirmed.
news.body:
A robot arm must pick the green ball instead of two red ones and put it in a basket. Simon Cowling of Denmark's fysical.ai tested four programs controlling that arm. They all learned from the same 50 demonstrations by a person.

The researcher then dimmed the room substantially. In normal light, 20 attempts out of 40 succeeded; in low light, 19 out of 40 succeeded. It would be tempting to say that darkness hardly mattered. But first we need to check what the cameras actually recorded.

The front camera's pictures became only 3% dimmer, even though light at the table fell roughly elevenfold. The camera on the arm recorded pictures 19% dimmer. Afterward, the author found automatic exposure enabled: the cameras could adjust how they collected light.

That setting probably helped, but no separate comparison switched the automatic control off. The test therefore did not show how the programs handle genuinely dark pictures. Camera settings matter here because the program receives its pictures through the camera, rather than seeing the room directly.

news.title: A robot uses what happened to a cable before
news.summary: University of Bologna researchers compared ways to shape a cable on a table. Records of earlier movements helped control it, while a better prediction did not always lead to a better action.
news.details: Bologna researchers compared ways to control a cable. One used stiffness, how hard it is to bend, and friction, which resists sliding; another used up to five previous movements and the shape changes they caused.
news.technical_novelty: University of Bologna researchers compared ways to shape a cable on a table. Records of earlier movements helped control it, while a better prediction did not always lead to a better action.
news.engineering_impact: Each trial allowed up to ten actions. Required accuracy meant cable points were, on average, no more than a centimeter from their targets, not that every point matched perfectly. The study only tested shaping on a plane. A person reset the cable, so starting shapes were not exactly identical across comparisons.
news.limitations: Each trial allowed up to ten actions. Required accuracy meant cable points were, on average, no more than a centimeter from their targets, not that every point matched perfectly. The study only tested shaping on a plane. A person reset the cable, so starting shapes were not exactly identical across comparisons.
news.evidence_status: The researchers describe their own tests. Repetition by another team has not been confirmed.
news.body:
Imagine a cable on a table that needs to match a target shape. Pulling one spot changes more than that spot alone. University of Bologna researchers tested what information helps a robot choose where to grasp and how to move.

One program used estimates of stiffness and friction. Stiffness describes how hard the cable is to bend; friction resists sliding along the table. Another program used up to five earlier movements and the changes in shape they produced.

The programs learned in computer experiments first. Researchers then moved them to a real robot without extra training on that robot. The version using previous interactions reached the required accuracy more often: in 88.3% of trials, compared with 76.7% for a version using shape alone.

Each trial allowed up to ten actions. Required accuracy meant cable points were, on average, no more than a centimeter from their targets, not that every point matched perfectly. The study only tested shaping on a plane. A person reset the cable, so starting shapes were not exactly identical across comparisons.

news.title: A robot waits for a truck in a computer-built yard
news.summary: Japan's Space Data created a hypothetical construction yard with people, robots and vehicles. Inside the program, users can examine where participants need to wait for one another.
news.details: Space Data placed a hypothetical construction yard on terrain around Hachioji Junction. Its program includes ten workers and fourteen robots, with adjustable numbers and tasks for comparing movement arrangements.
news.technical_novelty: Japan's Space Data created a hypothetical construction yard with people, robots and vehicles. Inside the program, users can examine where participants need to wait for one another.
news.engineering_impact: A safe route on screen does not prove that a physical robot will follow it safely. Some machine properties are estimates because exact values are not public. Nor does this announcement plan that construction at the junction: the company explicitly says the work is hypothetical.
news.limitations: A safe route on screen does not prove that a physical robot will follow it safely. Some machine properties are estimates because exact values are not public. Nor does this announcement plan that construction at the junction: the company explicitly says the work is hypothetical.
news.evidence_status: The company itself reports the tests, specifications or plans. The announcement supplies no independent verification.
news.body:
A truck approaches, and a robot stops to wait. This is not a report from a real construction site. Japan's Space Data built a simulation, a computer experiment showing people and machines working in a shared space.

The terrain comes from the real Hachioji Junction, but the construction yard is invented. It includes ten workers, fourteen robots, cranes and construction vehicles. Users can change participant numbers and tasks to examine whether there is enough space for movement and work.

According to the company, the program predicts where a vehicle will be 2.5 seconds later. A virtual robot waits for it to pass and avoids going under a suspended load. The system also calculates cable tension and load swing, rather than merely drawing a moving picture.

A safe route on screen does not prove that a physical robot will follow it safely. Some machine properties are estimates because exact values are not public. Nor does this announcement plan that construction at the junction: the company explicitly says the work is hypothetical.

technology_signal.title: Lights off. What did the robot see?
technology_signal.summary: A researcher dimmed the room where a robot moved a ball into a basket. One recorded view barely became darker, probably because of the cameras’ automatic settings.
technology_signal.implications: To find out whether a program handles a dark picture, switching off a lamp is not enough. The picture itself must be checked: a camera can brighten it before sending it to the robot.
